column1: # Recovery tier policy.  table<TAB>tier<TAB>reason
# TIER A — data lives in the primary artifact (full.dump). Restorable in one
#          pg_restore, scratch-verified, constraint-validated.
# TIER B — data lives in separate per-table archives streamed to an INDEPENDENT
#          filesystem. The primary artifact still carries the table's SCHEMA, so
#          a tier-A restore yields a structurally complete database with these
#          tables empty, and each archive is replayed into it afterwards.
# DEFAULT IS TIER A. A table absent from this file gets its data backed up. That
# is the fail-safe direction: forgetting to classify a new table costs disk, not
# data. Only an explicit line moves a table to tier B, and every such line has to
# say why.
# HARD RULES, enforced by the backup script and the cutover gate:
#   * a table named in RECOVERY_AUTHORITY_TABLES may never be tier B;
#   * a tier-B table must be append-only with an indexed monotonic chunk key;
#   * a tier-B table must have ZERO inbound foreign keys. This is not a style
#     rule: pg_restore adds FK constraints AFTER loading data, so restoring a
#     tier-A artifact whose child rows reference an absent tier-B parent fails
#     constraint validation and the artifact is not restorable at all. Proven
#     the hard way — a production scratch restore died on
#     meta_account_daily_source_snapshot_id_fkey because meta_raw_snapshots was
#     tier B. It has 8 inbound FKs; shopify_raw_snapshots has 7. Both are now
#     tier A. The config trio has zero, which is why it can be tiered;
#   * a tier-B table's archive must validate on count AND sha256 before the
#     backup is reported successful;
#   * a tier-B table that the pending migration MUTATES is refused — rollback
#     would then depend on tier B, which defeats the split.
# Why these five, and only these five (measured 2026-07-27 against production):
# they are 62.6 of the 136 GiB. Each was classified independently. NONE of them is
# provider-rebuildable — every one is a point-in-time observation the provider
# will not re-serve, so tier B is an ARCHIVE, never a discard. The split is
# justified purely by the proven migration write-set: the migration adds columns
# and indexes to them and mutates no pre-existing column, so a migration
# rollback never needs their rows.
# Chunk keys verified indexed:
#   meta_raw_snapshots        (fetched_at, id)  idx_meta_raw_snapshots_retention
#   shopify_raw_snapshots     (fetched_at, id)  idx_shopify_raw_snapshots_retention
#   meta_config_snapshots     id                primary key
#   meta_campaign_config_history  id            primary key
#   meta_adset_config_history     id            primary key
meta_config_snapshots
column3: 21.3 GiB / 22.4M rows. Append-only; no production DELETE exists. Migration touches it with ZERO statements. Read as an all-time bid-regime aggregate and for previous-different diffs, so the archive is mandatory for DR.

column1: meta_campaign_config_history
column3: 20.9 GiB / 23.2M rows (14.0 GiB of it index, which never enters a dump). Append-only, ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. Migration only DROPs a skip-unchanged trigger. Read at a decision cutoff by the ad decision engine, so the archive is mandatory for DR.

column1: meta_adset_config_history
column3: 20.4 GiB / 21.2M rows (12.9 GiB index). Same shape as the campaign table; also the only home of promoted_object_json and pixel_id.
